children: Reporting, Photography and Video by Dawn Gilbertson
LOS ANGELES-I was eating my second piece of hot honey and cracked black-pepper bacon in American Airlines' Flagship Lounge when an employee popped by.
"Did you see my text?" she asked.
I hadn't. My flight from LAX to Chicago was slightly delayed due to a late arriving aircraft, the message said, so sit tight.
You, too, can get hand-delivered flight updates if you pay hundreds of dollars for American's Five Star Service.

American, Delta and United each offer under-the-radar VIP services at select airports for a fee. VIPs for a day get a taste of the frictionless life enjoyed by travelers with the airlines' invite-only loyalty statuses like American's ConciergeKey. And you pay less than it costs for one of those private VIP terminals.
Celebrities and executives are big customers. On my American flight, a popular character actress booked it and was greeted in the jet bridge upon deplaning.
I tested all three services to see if they're worth it. As always, The Wall Street Journal paid all expenses and the airlines weren't notified in advance.
American Five Star Service
The American agent I booked the service with joked his mother is so spoiled by Five Star she won't fly without it. "And I don't even get a discount," he said.

American's service appears to be the least expensive of the three, starting at $350 or 35,000 miles, for the first adult. (There's also a $650 option called Five Star Select that comes with even more perks.)

But there's a catch. You can only reserve either Five Star option if you have a first-class or business-class ticket. Delta and United don't have this restriction, but Delta doesn't allow basic-economy passengers.
My first class ticket from LAX to Chicago was $788.
A lot of the VIP experience rides on your escort/greeter and how busy things are at the airport. I lucked out on both fronts.

My greeter, Tara, reached out the morning of my flight via text and told me exactly where to get dropped off. She and another employee were waiting at the curb, the latter grabbing my bag. Check-in at the private Flagship First desk was a breeze. Then we were off to a priority security line and lounge.

The basic Five Star service comes with Admirals Club access, but Tara dropped me off at the swankier Flagship lounge because it wasn't busy. You typically only get access to this lounge with the Five Star Select package, or if you're flying in a Flagship cabin.

The construction at LAX also worked in my favor. There's a long walk through a tunnel to many American gates and greeters try to arrange a car if one is available, a perk typically only guaranteed if you buy Five Star Select.
My ride to the plane: a black Ford Expedition. Tara took me up the jet bridge stairs to board.
Delta VIP Select
I booked Delta's VIP departure service at New York's JFK for $700. The booking agent promised I wouldn't have to think. "Someone will just be there to do everything," she said.
It was raining when I arrived. My greeter, Natalee, texted me to take my time getting out of the vehicle.

She was waiting at the curb with a priority bag tag and wheeled my bag into the cordoned off Delta One check-in area. I wasn't flying in Delta One, the airline's priciest premium cabin, but you get some of the perks with VIP Select.

I was supposed to get a ride in a Porsche to the Delta Sky Club, but they weren't running because of the rain. So we hopped in a standard-issue cart for a four-minute drive to the Delta Sky Club near gate A8. (Delta One ticket holders are taken to the Delta One lounge.)

Natalee escorted me to a roped-off section of the lounge and told me she'd "take her heels off and come running" if I needed anything. There was little exclusive about the space beyond nicer chairs. The room to spread out was nice, but it was awkward when other passengers walked in and were turned back.

Mauricio Parise, the Delta vice president who oversees the VIP Select program, says this isn't for show but to guarantee space for VIPs who choose to visit the lounge. Most don't, he says. Overall, they want to show up late and be whisked through security to the plane.
"They're seeking the private-jet-like experience," he says.
I saw Natalee again when she picked me up to walk to my gate. We would have taken a Porsche if I was in a different gate area, she said.

Just before boarding she found a better aisle seat for me without me asking. But when it was time for priority boarding she was on the phone with a couple of employees so I had to stand up to catch her attention. (Unlike other greeters, she is a supervisor and was juggling other duties that day. Delta says this isn't the norm and apologized.)
For $700, I'd want the full treatment next time.
United Signature Service

United is an outlier in my test because it outsources its service to Global Airport Concierge, which offers services at airports around the world. (The airline says it has a program similar to American's and Delta's for $650, but it's only available through corporate travel agencies.)

I paid $400 for VIP service from Chicago. My escort, Anisa, reached out early that morning via text to ask about my arrival time. She met me at the Terminal 1 curb and we walked to Premier check-in for bag drop-off. The TSA PreCheck lines were long so we went through an employee/wheelchair accessible lane.

We headed for the United Club but when I scanned my boarding pass at the e-gate it didn't let me through. United says my greeter should have talked to the front desk for easy admission with my package. I paid $59 for a day pass to access the lounge, which they are refunding.
Anisa met me outside the lounge before departure and walked me to my gate. My boarding group was five but I jumped to group one with the VIP service. Anisa said goodbye there.

I felt a little like an unaccompanied minor with this service and it wasn't worth $400 to me. But the parents of an 18-year-old whom Anisa escorted earlier in the week probably were buying peace of mind.

I wouldn't personally pay for any of these since I have every airport security fast-pass as well as lounge access and no need for privacy. But American's Five Star service sure would be a nice splurge for a special occasion or for the non-frequent fliers in your life. (Don't get any ideas, Mom.)
